currencies.headline: Sterling holds steady as a light UK calendar leaves it taking cues from the dollar.
currencies.commentary:
Sterling has traded in a tight range through the Asian and early European sessions, holding broadly steady after last week's Bank of England decision. Policymakers held Bank Rate at 3.75% on 30 July, the fifth hold of the year, but the split vote flagged growing unease among some committee members about upside inflation risks. That split has left traders reluctant to push sterling decisively in either direction ahead of this morning's UK services PMI, with the currency instead taking most of its direction from broader dollar sentiment.

The pound remains well supported against the euro, sitting near one-year highs on the back of a roughly 150 basis point gap between Bank of England and European Central Bank policy rates, one of the widest advantages sterling has held over its European counterpart in years. That rate differential continues to underpin demand for the currency even as UK growth data stays soft, though with three MPC members already pushing for higher rates, further tightening looks unlikely near term, meaning sterling's next real test comes from how quickly UK inflation cools relative to its peers.
currencies.watchToday: The UK's final services PMI for July is due this morning, watched for confirmation of the flash estimate's rebound to 51.8 after June's contraction to a two-year low. With no Bank of England meeting this week, sterling's bigger tests come from this evening's FOMC minutes and Friday's US jobs report.

currencies.headline: Euro steady but capped by a widening rate gap with the pound and firmer core inflation.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has traded in a narrow band overnight, with little fresh domestic catalyst to shift sentiment either way. Final eurozone services and composite PMI readings due this morning are expected to broadly confirm last month's flash estimates, offering only a modest update on the bloc's underlying growth momentum. The bigger recent talking point has been July's flash inflation print, where core price growth came in firmer than expected, complicating the European Central Bank's path just as policymakers elsewhere, including the Bank of England, hold a clear rate advantage over the eurozone.

That roughly 150 basis point gap between Bank of England and ECB policy rates has been a persistent drag on the euro against sterling, and firmer core inflation gives the ECB less room to ease further without risking a repeat of last year's price pressures. This morning's producer price data for June will be watched as a leading indicator of where consumer inflation heads next, feeding into how much patience the ECB can afford. For now the single currency looks more like a bystander to the dollar's swings than a currency with strong independent direction of its own.
currencies.watchToday: Eurozone final services and composite PMI for July and producer prices for June are due this morning, both broadly secondary releases. The bigger events for the euro this week are Thursday's Eurozone retail sales and German industrial production on Friday.

currencies.headline: Dollar softer as easing Middle East tensions dim safe-haven demand ahead of a data-heavy day.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has drifted lower across major pairs this morning as easing tensions between the US and Iran take some safe-haven bid out of the currency, with broader risk appetite improving as a result. That softer tone follows last week's Federal Reserve decision, where policymakers held the target range at 3.50 to 3.75% in a 9-3 vote, though notably three regional presidents dissented in favour of a quarter point hike, the first coordinated hawkish dissent of its kind in a decade. Today's session brings the ADP employment report and the closely watched ISM Services PMI, both seen as previews of Friday's nonfarm payrolls.

That hawkish split at the Fed is unusual and reflects genuine disagreement about how much further the labour market needs to cool before rates can safely come down, a debate reopened by June's weak payrolls print of just 57,000 jobs. This evening's release of the minutes from that meeting should reveal how deep the divide really runs, with markets on alert for any signal about the conditions needed for the Fed's next move under Chair Kevin Warsh. A second soft jobs report on Friday would add fuel to the doves' case and likely weigh further on the dollar.
currencies.watchToday: A busy US session: ADP employment and the ISM Services PMI this afternoon, followed by the FOMC's July meeting minutes this evening and remarks from Fed Governor Lisa Cook. All eyes then turn to Friday's nonfarm payrolls, the week's key release after June's surprisingly weak print.

currencies.headline: Yen stays on the back foot as wide yield gaps keep carry trades in favour.
currencies.commentary:
The yen remains under pressure this morning, continuing a stretch of underperformance driven by the widening gap between US and Japanese government bond yields. That spread has stretched further in recent weeks as markets price in the possibility of additional Fed rate hikes, making it more attractive to borrow in yen and invest in higher yielding dollar assets, a dynamic that keeps steady downward pressure on the currency regardless of what the Bank of Japan does domestically. This morning's minutes from the BoJ's June meeting and the final services PMI are unlikely to shift that picture much on their own.

The irony is that the Bank of Japan has actually turned more hawkish, holding its policy rate at 1.00% at July's meeting in an 8-1 vote while upgrading its economic outlook and warning that core inflation could overshoot its 2% target near term. That should, in theory, support the currency, but as long as US yields stay elevated relative to Japan's, the carry trade dynamic tends to dominate. A softer than expected US jobs report on Friday, easing the pressure on Treasury yields, is probably the yen's best near term hope for relief.
currencies.watchToday: Only low-impact releases for the yen today: BoJ June meeting minutes and the final services PMI. The bigger date is Thursday's wage and household spending data, watched by the Bank of Japan as a gauge of whether consumption can sustain the inflation outlook.

currencies.headline: Franc softer as easing geopolitical risk trims safe-haven demand.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has eased back a touch this morning as easing US-Iran tensions reduce some of the safe-haven demand that had supported the currency through recent bouts of geopolitical anxiety. With no domestic data due today, the franc is largely taking its cues from the broader shift in risk appetite rather than anything happening at home, leaving it a relatively quiet mover within the G10 basket this morning.

The Swiss National Bank has held its policy rate at zero since March and is widely expected to stay there through year end, with July inflation slipping to just 0.4% year on year, its softest reading in four months and comfortably within the SNB's target. That gives policymakers little urgent reason to act in either direction, though officials have signalled readiness to intervene in currency markets should renewed franc strength start to threaten the export sector, a live concern given how much of Swiss industry depends on a competitive exchange rate. For now the more likely path is a further cyclical easing in the franc's safe-haven premium as regional tensions cool.
currencies.watchToday: No Swiss data due today. Thursday brings the unemployment rate for July, watched for further signs of strain in the export sector, but the franc's next real test is the SNB's September policy meeting.

currencies.headline: Loonie softer as oil slips on hopes of an Iran deal easing supply risk.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has weakened this morning as crude oil prices extend their recent slide, falling toward the mid-70s per barrel amid growing optimism that progress in US-Iran talks could ease the supply risk premium that had been supporting energy prices. For an economy as reliant on energy exports as Canada's, a sustained pullback in oil tends to translate fairly directly into a softer currency, and that dynamic has been the dominant driver for the loonie over the past several sessions rather than anything domestic.

With the Bank of Canada on hold until its September meeting and no major domestic data due today, the loonie is left almost entirely at the mercy of oil prices and the broader dollar tone. That makes Friday's Canadian jobs report, released alongside the US nonfarm payrolls figure, the next real domestic catalyst, watched for how much slack is building in the labour market. Until then, expect the currency to keep tracking crude prices and shifts in risk appetite more closely than any home-grown story.
currencies.watchToday: No major Canadian data due today. Friday's Labour Force Survey, released alongside the US jobs report, is the week's key release, with markets watching for signs of slack building ahead of the Bank of Canada's September meeting.

currencies.headline: Kiwi firm as rate hike expectations build ahead of September's RBNZ decision.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has held onto recent gains this morning, extending a firmer run built on rising expectations that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand will follow July's rate hike, its first in three years, with another move in September. That repricing follows yesterday's stronger than expected inflation data, with annual inflation accelerating to 4.1% in the second quarter, above both market expectations and the RBNZ's own forecast, reinforcing recent warnings from the Bank's chief economist about persistent price pressure.

Sentiment has also been helped by a broader improvement in risk appetite as Middle East tensions ease, a backdrop that tends to favour higher-yielding, growth-sensitive currencies like the kiwi. With markets now pricing in a further quarter point hike as close to fully priced for September, the currency's near term path looks more dependent on how incoming data confirms or challenges that view than on any single release. Yesterday's quarterly employment figures, which showed a still-resilient labour market, added to the case for the RBNZ to keep tightening.
currencies.watchToday: No major New Zealand data due today, following yesterday's employment report. Thursday's RBNZ inflation expectations survey is a secondary release, with attention really focused on the Reserve Bank's September policy meeting where another rate hike is widely expected.

currencies.headline: Aussie caught between a supportive RBA and an uneven Chinese recovery.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar is trading in a holding pattern this morning, with no domestic data due and traders still weighing two competing forces. The Reserve Bank of Australia's cash rate has been left unchanged with a clear wait-and-see tone, and markets currently assign only around a one-in-four chance of a hike this month, rising to better than even odds by December, a backdrop that is broadly supportive relative to peers still cutting rates.

Working against that is China's uneven recovery: second quarter growth of 4.3% year on year masked a split picture, with industrial production up a solid 5.3% but retail sales growth of just 1.0% and fixed asset investment down 5.7% in the first half. Given China's role as Australia's largest trading partner, soft Chinese consumer demand and weak construction activity temper the currency's upside even when domestic rate settings are favourable. Thursday's Australian trade balance data will be watched for fresh evidence of how that China relationship is holding up.
currencies.watchToday: No major Australian data today. Thursday's trade balance for June is the next domestic release, watched given China's status as Australia's top trading partner, while broader sentiment continues to hinge on the RBA's rate path and Chinese demand signals.

currencies.headline: Offshore yuan steady near multi-year strength as the PBoC leans supportive.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has held close to its strongest levels since February 2023 this morning, with only modest moves as investors digest fresh signals from the People's Bank of China aimed at supporting growth. The central bank has reaffirmed its accommodative policy stance, pledging to keep liquidity ample and fine-tune tools as needed, even as a private sector survey showed factory activity slowing to a four month low in July, a reminder that underlying momentum in the real economy remains soft even as the currency itself stays firm.

That combination, currency strength alongside manufacturing weakness, reflects deliberate policy choices as much as market forces: Beijing has been pushing initiatives to internationalise the yuan, including expanding offshore trading pilots and strengthening Shanghai and Hong Kong's roles as offshore renminbi hubs, which has helped underpin demand for the currency independent of the domestic growth picture. This morning's services PMI reading rounds out the picture of Chinese demand and carries some relevance for the Australian and New Zealand dollars given their trade exposure to China.
currencies.watchToday: The RatingDog China services PMI for July is due this morning, a secondary release that nonetheless feeds into the broader China demand picture relevant for AUD and NZD. Friday's trade balance is the bigger event this week, watched after June's near record surplus driven by chip and AI hardware exports.

currencies.headline: Rand steadies as a softer dollar offsets lingering inflation concerns.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has found some support this morning as broader dollar softness and easing global risk aversion provide relief after a difficult few sessions. The currency had come under pressure following the South African Reserve Bank's decision to hold its repo rate at 7% on 23 July, a split 4-2 vote in which two committee members pushed for a further increase, underscoring ongoing unease about the inflation backdrop.

That unease is well founded: annual inflation accelerated to 5.0% in June, its highest level in two years, with core inflation also picking up to 4.1%, both readings running above the upper end of the SARB's target range. That combination of a cautious, divided central bank and inflation running hot leaves the rand vulnerable to renewed selling pressure whenever global risk appetite sours, even as today's calmer backdrop offers some near term relief. With no major domestic data due, the currency is likely to keep trading on broader dollar sentiment and commodity price swings rather than any home-grown catalyst.
currencies.watchToday: No major South African data due today or later this week; the rand is likely to keep trading on broader dollar sentiment and global risk appetite rather than a domestic catalyst, with the SARB's next policy decision not due until September.

currencies.headline: Sterling drifts sideways with no domestic catalysts, leaving the dollar in the driving seat.
currencies.commentary:
Sterling has traded in a narrow range through the Asian and early European sessions, with little independent direction as this week's UK calendar stays light. Monday's steep downward revision to the final manufacturing PMI, which fell to a four month low, was absorbed calmly given the survey's relatively minor market impact and a broadly softer dollar backdrop. This morning's only domestic releases, the BRC Shop Price Index and the BRC-KPMG Retail Sales Monitor for July, are both low impact gauges that rarely move the currency on their own, so sterling continues to take its cues almost entirely from the greenback and shifting rate expectations abroad.

That dependence on external drivers reflects a genuine gap in this week's UK data and policy calendar: there is no Bank of England meeting scheduled and nothing of real weight due until later in the week. With domestic catalysts thin, sterling's fate this week rests largely on how Friday's US employment report and the ongoing fallout from Japan's currency intervention shape broader dollar sentiment. A steadier dollar would likely keep sterling range bound, while renewed dollar weakness could let it drift higher almost by default.
currencies.watchToday: Only low-impact UK retail data is due today, the BRC Shop Price Index and Retail Sales Monitor for July, unlikely to move sterling meaningfully. With no BoE meeting this week, attention stays on Friday's US jobs report and the broader dollar tone.

currencies.headline: Euro holds its hawkish-driven gains as accelerating inflation keeps a September ECB hike in play.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has held firm this morning, consolidating recent gains built on last week's hotter than expected July inflation reading, which showed price growth accelerating for a second straight month to its highest level since the ECB's tightening cycle began. Monday's final manufacturing PMI confirmed the strongest reading since April, with German factory output at a four year high, reinforcing the sense that the currency bloc's recovery has some genuine momentum behind it even as energy costs remain elevated.

The driving force remains the energy linked inflation surge tied to the renewed Middle East conflict, which has pushed headline eurozone inflation further above the ECB's target and left markets pricing a meaningful probability of another rate hike at September's meeting, a striking reversal from the rate cut expectations that prevailed just a few months ago. That repricing has been the single biggest support for the euro this summer, and it leaves the currency more sensitive than usual to any further oil price swings or comments from ECB officials hinting at the path beyond September.
currencies.watchToday: No major eurozone data is scheduled today. With the ECB's next decision not until September, the euro is likely to keep trading on the broader inflation and oil price narrative, alongside any spillover from the yen intervention story and Friday's US jobs report.

currencies.headline: Dollar stays on the back foot as intervention jitters and soft labour signals weigh.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar remains under modest pressure this morning, still digesting the fallout from last week's coordinated intervention to support the yen and a run of US data that has done little to dispel expectations of further Federal Reserve easing. The greenback made up some ground on Monday after a surprisingly strong ISM manufacturing reading, the best since 2022, but has struggled to build on that bounce as traders stay wary of further central bank action to cap the dollar's recent strength against Japan's currency.

The bigger story for the dollar this week is the labour market. June's payrolls report undershot expectations badly, and today's JOLTS job openings and factory orders data will be parsed for further evidence of cooling demand ahead of Friday's more consequential July jobs report. A second weak print would reinforce the case for a near term rate cut and likely extend the dollar's softer tone, while a stabilisation would give the currency some room to recover lost ground against its major peers.
currencies.watchToday: US JOLTS job openings and factory orders for June are due this afternoon at 15:00 UK time, both feeding into the broader labour market picture. The main event remains Friday's US jobs report for July, which will be the key test of whether the recent softening in hiring is continuing.

currencies.headline: Yen holds the bulk of its intervention-driven surge as markets brace for round two.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has stayed firm through the morning, retaining most of the sharp gains built up over the past several sessions after Japan's historic joint intervention with Washington to support the currency. Having touched its strongest level in three months last week, the yen has eased back only modestly from those highs, with traders still on alert for further coordinated action given how large and deliberate the initial operation was.

The key question now is whether the yen can extend its advance meaningfully further or whether it settles back into a more gradual grind, given that the underlying drivers, a still cautious Bank of Japan and negative real interest rates, have not changed as much as the scale of the intervention might suggest. The BoJ's decision to hold rates steady last week, in an 8-1 vote, means the currency is being supported more by intervention risk and positioning than by a genuine shift in monetary fundamentals, which leaves it vulnerable to a renewed slide if authorities step back.
currencies.watchToday: No major Japanese data is scheduled today. The market's focus stays on intervention risk and any signals from Japanese officials about further action, with the yen's ability to hold its recent gains the key thing to watch this week.

currencies.headline: Franc's safe-haven bid eases slightly as Middle East tensions show signs of cooling.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has softened a touch this morning after weeks of being underpinned by demand for havens amid the Middle East conflict, as signs of de-escalation and a further pullback in oil prices take some urgency out of the safety trade. The currency remains close to some of its strongest levels in years, but the easing in geopolitical risk premium has taken a little of the edge off the recent bid.

Monday's Swiss inflation data showed price growth easing further to a very low level, with core inflation steady, underlining just how little domestic pressure there is behind the franc's strength. This is a currency moving almost entirely on external, safe-haven flows rather than its own fundamentals. The Swiss National Bank has said it sees little reason to intervene for now despite the franc's strength, but has made clear it stands ready to act if the safe-haven bid resumes in earnest, a threshold that stays firmly in view given how quickly the Middle East situation has flared up and cooled in recent months.
currencies.watchToday: No Swiss data is scheduled today. The franc is likely to keep trading on the broader safe-haven flow, taking its cues from Middle East headlines and oil prices, with the SNB's next policy decision not due until September.

currencies.headline: Loonie under pressure as oil extends its slide on Middle East de-escalation.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has softened this morning as crude oil prices continue to fall sharply, extending Monday's steep decline as diplomatic momentum between Washington and Tehran and a recovery in tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz strip out much of the war related premium that had been supporting prices. As one of the world's major oil exporters, Canada's currency remains highly sensitive to swings in crude, and the scale of this pullback has been enough to outweigh the loonie's recent recovery.

The mechanism is straightforward: lower oil prices mean lower expected export revenues and terms of trade for Canada, which typically translates into a softer currency, and that link has dominated the loonie's price action over the past week regardless of the domestic data backdrop. Today's June merchandise trade balance will offer a read on how cross border demand held up before this latest oil move, but with crude remaining the dominant driver day to day, its influence on the currency is likely to be secondary unless it surprises significantly.
currencies.watchToday: Canada's merchandise trade balance for June is due at 13:30 UK time, a secondary release given oil's dominant role in driving the currency right now. Further Middle East headlines and the path of crude prices remain the more important thing to watch this week.

currencies.headline: Kiwi steadies ahead of a pivotal labour market test.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has traded in a tight range this morning, holding most of its recent gains as traders position ahead of today's second quarter employment report, arguably the most important scheduled release of the week for the currency. The kiwi has been one of the stronger performers among the majors recently, supported by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's hawkish tilt after its latest rate hike and a jump in domestic consumer confidence, even as some of that momentum was tempered by softer Chinese data earlier in the week.

Today's employment data matters because it will help confirm whether the labour market can withstand further RBNZ tightening without cracking, a question that sits right at the heart of how much room the central bank has to keep raising rates. Economists expect the unemployment rate to tick up slightly from the first quarter, and a reading in line with or better than that would likely reinforce the kiwi's hawkish policy support, while a sharper deterioration could quickly unwind some of its recent gains.
currencies.watchToday: New Zealand's second quarter employment change and unemployment rate land late tonight at 23:45 UK time, the standout event for the kiwi this week given the RBNZ's next policy statement isn't due until early September. A stronger than expected labour market would reinforce the case for further tightening, while a soft print would raise doubts about how much further the RBNZ can go.

currencies.headline: Aussie stays range-bound as fading rate-hike bets meet a wobbly China backdrop.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has traded without much direction this morning, caught between two competing forces: a China manufacturing survey that eased further and disappointed expectations earlier in the week, and a domestic inflation picture that has all but ruled out a Reserve Bank of Australia rate hike at its meeting next week. Given how closely Australian trade and commodity exports track Chinese industrial demand, the softer PMI data has been a persistent headwind, while the fading prospect of higher local rates has removed a source of support that had been building through the RBA's more hawkish commentary earlier in the year.

That combination, cooler China data and a central bank that now looks set to hold rather than hike, largely explains why the Aussie has struggled to build any real momentum in either direction over the past week. Confirmation, or a contradiction, of the official Chinese PMI reading is likely to come from China's Caixin survey, which skews toward smaller, export oriented firms and often diverges from the official gauge, making it a genuine swing factor for sentiment toward the currency in the days ahead.
currencies.watchToday: No Australian data is scheduled today. The RBA's next policy decision on 11 August is the key event for the week ahead, with markets now largely expecting a hold given the latest inflation figures, alongside any further signals from Chinese data on the health of Australia's largest trading partner.

currencies.headline: Yuan holds recent gains as PBoC manages the pace of appreciation.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has been broadly steady this morning, consolidating a run of gains that has taken the currency to some of its firmest levels against the dollar in well over a year. The People's Bank of China has continued to set its daily reference rate at levels that suggest policymakers are comfortable with gradual strength but wary of letting the currency run too far too fast, a pattern that has been evident in the fixing for much of the past several weeks.

The broader backdrop remains supportive: Chinese exports have held up reasonably well and the central bank has reiterated that it intends to keep the currency basically stable at a reasonable and balanced level through the second half of the year, language that points to continued management rather than either a sharp appreciation or a renewed bout of weakness. This week's softer factory PMI readings have introduced a note of caution, a reminder that the underlying growth picture is not without its wobbles, but so far that has done little to derail the yuan's gradual upward drift.
currencies.watchToday: No major Chinese data is scheduled for release today. Markets will continue watching the PBoC's daily fixing for signals on how much further appreciation authorities are willing to tolerate, alongside any follow-through from this week's mixed manufacturing PMI readings.

currencies.headline: Rand steadies after its recent slide, but August's seasonal headwinds keep sentiment cautious.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has found a firmer footing this morning after recovering from a multi month low touched last week, helped by the broader improvement in risk appetite as oil prices fall back and global tensions ease. That recovery has been welcome, but it comes against a backdrop of genuine domestic caution following the South African Reserve Bank's decision last month to hold its policy rate, a split decision that saw two of the six committee members push for a further increase given how far inflation has drifted above target.

Annual inflation accelerated to its highest level in two years in June, with core inflation also running above the top of the SARB's target band, leaving the central bank in a genuinely difficult spot: growth remains fragile, but price pressures argue against cutting rates any time soon. Layered on top of that is a well documented seasonal pattern in which the rand has historically been one of the weaker performers in August, so while today's tone is steadier, the combination of elevated inflation and seasonal headwinds means the currency's recent recovery should be treated as fragile rather than a genuine turn in trend.
currencies.watchToday: No major South African data is scheduled today. With the SARB's next meeting still some weeks away, the rand is likely to keep trading on broader risk sentiment and oil prices, against the seasonal backdrop of August historically being a weak month for the currency.

currencies.headline: Sterling drifts through a quiet afternoon, still leaning on the dollar and broader risk mood for direction.
currencies.commentary:
There has been no fresh UK-specific news since this morning, and sterling's afternoon has been shaped almost entirely by outside forces. With equity markets extending their rally on hopes that Washington and Tehran can still reach a diplomatic outcome, the broader risk-on mood has given sterling a modest lift alongside other majors, helped further by a softer tone in the dollar. The move looks more like sterling riding a general wave than anything home-grown.

That pattern fits neatly with this morning's read: a genuinely quiet UK calendar leaves the pound almost entirely dependent on external drivers. With no Bank of England meeting this week and nothing of real weight left on today's domestic docket, sterling's next real test is Wednesday's final UK services PMI, followed by Friday's US jobs report, which will likely do more to set the pound's direction than anything the UK itself produces this week.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled domestically for the rest of today. Wednesday brings the final UK services PMI at 09:30 UK time, a useful check on whether last month's flash rebound holds, while Friday's US payrolls report remains the bigger swing factor given how thin the UK calendar is this week.

currencies.headline: Euro pushes to a fresh multi-week high after eurozone growth data beats forecasts by a wide margin.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has extended its advance this afternoon after data confirmed the eurozone economy grew at roughly twice the pace the market had expected last quarter, its strongest expansion in well over a year. Combined with the broader improvement in risk appetite as Middle East tensions show further signs of cooling, the single currency has pushed to its firmest level in several weeks, building on the hawkish, inflation-driven story that has supported it through the morning.

The growth beat reinforces the case markets have been building since last week's hot inflation print: that the ECB may need to raise rates again in September rather than cut, a striking reversal from where expectations sat only a few months ago. That combination of accelerating growth and above-target inflation leaves the euro unusually sensitive to anything that shifts the oil price or geopolitical backdrop between now and the ECB's next meeting.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further of note is due domestically for the rest of today. Wednesday brings the eurozone's final services PMI and June producer price data, both at 09:00 UK time, though with the ECB's next decision not until September, the euro is likely to keep taking its cues mainly from oil prices and the broader risk mood.

currencies.headline: Dollar softens against risk-sensitive peers as stocks rally, with a heavy afternoon of US data still to come.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has slipped a little further this afternoon as risk appetite has improved markedly, with equities extending Monday's tech-led rebound toward record territory on hopes that the Iran standoff can still be resolved diplomatically. That risk-on backdrop has typically been a headwind for the greenback against currencies like the euro and pound, even as gold has stayed firm, a sign that rate-cut expectations have not gone away despite the improved mood in stocks.

The bigger test comes later this afternoon, with US trade balance data due at 13:30 UK time followed by JOLTS job openings, factory orders and final durable goods orders at 15:00, and a fireside chat from Fed Vice Chair Michelle Bowman at 17:45. All of it will be read for clues on labour market health ahead of Friday's payrolls report, where the consensus has already been revised down since this morning, from around 130,000 to roughly 80,000 jobs, underlining how cautious the market has become on hiring.
currencies.watchToday: US trade balance lands at 13:30 UK time, followed by JOLTS job openings, factory orders and final durable goods orders at 15:00, and Fed Vice Chair Bowman's fireside chat at 17:45. All of it builds toward Friday's July jobs report, now expected to show a much softer roughly 80,000 gain.

currencies.headline: Yen gives back a little of its intervention-driven surge as the risk-on mood takes some shine off havens.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has eased modestly this afternoon as broader risk appetite improves, with easing Middle East tensions and a rallying stock market reducing some of the safe-haven demand that had been supporting the currency since Friday's coordinated intervention. Even so, the pullback looks minor set against the scale of last week's move, and the yen retains the large majority of the ground it gained when Japan and the United States stepped in together to halt its slide.

The underlying question has not changed since this morning: whether the yen's strength reflects a genuine shift in fundamentals or simply intervention risk and positioning. The Bank of Japan's cautious policy stance and negative real rates are unchanged, which means today's modest give-back is best read as risk sentiment washing through rather than a reassessment of Japan's rate outlook. Markets remain alert to the possibility of further coordinated action if the currency resumes sliding.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing is scheduled for the rest of today. Tomorrow brings the Bank of Japan's June meeting minutes at 00:50 UK time and the final services PMI at 01:30, though intervention risk and any comments from Japanese officials remain the dominant thing to watch this week.

currencies.headline: Franc's safe-haven bid continues to fade as easing Middle East tensions lift risk appetite further.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has softened a little further this afternoon, extending this morning's pullback as signs of a possible diplomatic path in the Middle East and a rallying stock market take more of the urgency out of the safe-haven trade. The franc remains close to its softest level against the dollar in more than a year, but today's move continues the gradual unwind of the safety premium that had built up over recent weeks of conflict-driven uncertainty.

With Swiss inflation already running at a very low level and the SNB signalling no immediate appetite to intervene, the franc is being driven almost entirely by external flows rather than anything domestic. That leaves it unusually exposed to the ebb and flow of Middle East headlines and oil prices: further de-escalation would likely extend today's softening, while any renewed flare-up could just as quickly bring the haven bid back.
currencies.watchToday: No Swiss data is scheduled for the rest of today or tomorrow. The franc is likely to keep trading almost entirely on Middle East headlines and oil prices, with the SNB's next policy decision not due until September.

currencies.headline: Loonie stays under pressure as oil extends a sharp slide, with Canadian trade data due within the hour.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has remained on the back foot this afternoon as crude oil extends a sharp decline, falling by roughly four to five percent on the day as diplomatic hopes over Iran and easing concern about Strait of Hormuz disruption strip more of the war premium out of the price. As one of the world's larger oil exporters, Canada's currency remains highly geared to swings in crude, and today's slide has been steep enough to keep the loonie soft even against a broadly weaker dollar.

The mechanism is the same one flagged this morning: cheaper oil means weaker expected export revenues and a softer terms-of-trade picture for Canada, and that link has dominated the currency's moves over the past week regardless of the domestic data. June's merchandise trade balance, due shortly, will offer a read on how cross-border demand held up before this latest oil move, but with crude setting the tone day to day, its impact on the loonie is likely to be secondary unless it surprises sharply.
currencies.watchToday: Canada's June merchandise trade balance is due at 13:30 UK time, alongside the US equivalent release at the same time. Oil prices and any further Middle East diplomatic headlines remain the dominant driver for the loonie for the rest of today and into tomorrow.

currencies.headline: Kiwi holds steady through a quiet afternoon, marking time ahead of tonight's pivotal employment data.
currencies.commentary:
Little has changed for the New Zealand dollar since this morning. It has traded in a tight range through the afternoon, drifting only slightly firmer alongside the broader improvement in risk appetite, with no domestic news to give it independent direction. Attention has shifted almost entirely to tonight's second quarter employment report, which stands as the standout release of the week for the currency.

The stakes are unchanged from this morning's preview: the data will help confirm whether New Zealand's labour market can absorb further Reserve Bank tightening without cracking, at a time when the RBNZ's hawkish tilt after its last hike has been one of the kiwi's main sources of support. Consensus looks for the unemployment rate to edge up to 5.4% from 5.3% in the first quarter; a reading at or better than that would likely reinforce the case for more tightening, while a sharper deterioration could quickly unwind some of the currency's recent gains.
currencies.watchToday: New Zealand's second quarter employment change and unemployment rate land at 23:45 UK time tonight, by far the standout event of the week for the kiwi given the RBNZ's next policy statement isn't due until early September. A stronger than expected print would support further tightening bets, while a weak one would raise doubts about how much further the RBNZ can go.

currencies.headline: Aussie drifts higher with the broader risk-on mood, still caught between fading rate-hike bets and a cautious China backdrop.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has firmed only modestly this afternoon, tracking the general improvement in risk appetite as equities rally and Middle East tensions show signs of cooling, rather than responding to any fresh domestic news. With no Australian data due today, the currency remains caught in the same tension flagged this morning: a China manufacturing backdrop that has been softening, against a domestic inflation picture that has all but ruled out a Reserve Bank of Australia rate hike next week.

That combination continues to cap the Aussie's upside even as broader sentiment improves, since a currency so exposed to Chinese industrial demand needs more than a global risk rally to build sustained momentum. The next real test of that China link comes from tomorrow's services PMI reading, which tends to skew toward smaller, export-oriented firms and can diverge meaningfully from the official gauge, making it a genuine swing factor for sentiment over the coming days.
currencies.watchToday: No Australian data is due for the rest of today. China's Services PMI lands early tomorrow at 02:45 UK time and will be watched closely given the trade linkage, with Australia's own June trade balance following on Thursday and the RBA's policy decision on 11 August the bigger event further out.

currencies.headline: Yuan holds close to its firmest levels in years as risk-on sentiment and orderly PBoC guidance keep the currency steady.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has been little changed this afternoon, holding near its strongest levels against the dollar in well over a year as the broader improvement in risk sentiment adds a further, if modest, layer of support. The People's Bank of China's daily reference rate has continued to signal comfort with gradual strength rather than either a rapid appreciation or a return to weakness, a pattern that has held steady through the session.

The wider backdrop is unchanged from this morning: Chinese exports have held up reasonably well, and policymakers have reiterated they intend to keep the currency broadly stable at a balanced level through the rest of the year. This week's softer factory PMI readings remain a note of caution about the underlying growth picture, but so far that has done little to disturb the yuan's steady, well-managed drift, with tomorrow's services survey the next data point likely to shape sentiment.
currencies.watchToday: China's RatingDog Services PMI for July is due tomorrow at 02:45 UK time, a useful cross-check on the softer factory readings seen this week. The more significant July trade balance follows on Friday; until then, the PBoC's daily fixing remains the main signal to watch.

currencies.headline: Rand extends its recovery as falling oil prices and improved risk appetite continue to support sentiment.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has continued to firm this afternoon, building on its recovery from last month's multi-month low as oil prices extend a sharp slide and broader risk appetite improves on hopes of Middle East de-escalation. As a net oil importer, South Africa benefits directly from cheaper crude through lower import costs and reduced inflation pressure, and that dynamic has been the main driver behind the rand's steadier tone since midday.

The recovery still sits against a genuinely cautious domestic backdrop, unchanged from this morning: annual inflation running at a two-year high, a South African Reserve Bank that held rates last month in a split decision, and August's well-documented seasonal tendency to be one of the weaker months for the currency. That combination means today's firmer tone is best read as a function of favourable external conditions rather than any resolution of the rand's underlying vulnerabilities, leaving the recovery fragile if oil or risk sentiment turn.
currencies.watchToday: No South African data is scheduled for the rest of today, and none appears on the calendar through the rest of this week. With the SARB's next meeting still some weeks away, the rand is likely to keep trading mainly on oil prices and broader risk sentiment, against the seasonal backdrop of August historically being a weak month for the currency.

currencies.headline: Sterling steady as the Bank of England settles into a holding pattern and traders lean on US data for direction.
currencies.commentary:
The pound has traded in a narrow range overnight and into this morning, with little fresh domestic news to push it either way. Last Thursday's Bank of England decision, a widely expected hold at 3.75% for a fifth consecutive meeting, came on a split vote that flagged upside inflation risks even as the move itself surprised no one. Today's calendar brings only the final July manufacturing PMI, a routine confirmation of the earlier flash estimate, so sterling is largely taking its cue from broader dollar sentiment and the overnight swings in oil prices tied to Middle East tensions.

The mechanism worth watching is the interest rate gap over the eurozone: UK CPI eased to 2.6% in June, but services inflation has stayed sticky, which is precisely why the Bank held rather than cut, and that yield advantage over the ECB continues to offer sterling some underlying support. With the Bank now sidelined until its next meeting, though, the pound has little of its own to trade on this week, leaving it more a passenger to the US dollar's own path, particularly into Friday's payrolls report, than a currency setting an independent course.
currencies.watchToday: Only the final UK manufacturing PMI for July is due today, a minor revision of the flash reading that rarely moves the currency much. With no Bank of England meeting scheduled this week, attention turns to Tuesday's construction PMI and Wednesday's services PMI for a fuller read on the domestic economy, alongside Friday's US jobs report, which is likely to matter more for sterling's near-term direction than anything on the UK docket.

currencies.headline: Euro finds support from a hawkish inflation surprise as traders push back bets on an ECB rate cut.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has held a firm tone this morning, building on last week's reaction to the flash Eurozone inflation print, where headline CPI rose to 2.9% year on year as expected but core inflation unexpectedly accelerated to 2.5% from June's 2.4%. That hawkish surprise, driven partly by a jump in energy costs following the latest flare up in Middle East tensions, has reinforced the view that the European Central Bank will stay on hold for longer than previously assumed. Today's calendar holds only the final July manufacturing PMI, a small revision to the earlier flash reading, leaving the single currency to trade mostly on the inflation story and on the broader dollar backdrop.

Why it matters: a central bank that is seen holding rates for longer typically offers more support to its currency, and the core inflation surprise complicates any near-term case for eurozone rate cuts even as growth in the bloc remains modest. That shift in expectations has been a key reason the euro has held its ground against the dollar recently, though the currency remains sensitive to how US data, and any further escalation in oil markets, shape the broader risk backdrop this week.
currencies.watchToday: Today brings only the final Eurozone manufacturing PMI for July, a routine confirmation of the flash estimate that is rarely a significant mover on its own. The bigger releases this week are Wednesday's final services and composite PMIs, Wednesday's producer price data, and Thursday's retail sales figures, all of which will help confirm or challenge last week's hawkish inflation surprise.

currencies.headline: Dollar steadies after its roughest week in three months as traders await a fresh batch of US data.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has firmed modestly this morning after last week's broad-based slide, which at one point took the currency to its softest level since mid-June before a Friday rebound trimmed the damage. The Federal Reserve held its policy rate unchanged for a fifth consecutive meeting, with Chair Kevin Warsh offering little fresh guidance on the path ahead, though markets continue to price roughly a two-thirds probability of a rate move at the September meeting given persistent inflation pressures. Today's session brings the first major US data point of the week, the ISM manufacturing PMI for July, with consensus looking for a pickup to 54.0 from June's confirmed 53.3 reading.

The dollar's recent wobble reflects genuine uncertainty over the Fed's next move: with inflation risks still elevated, partly from the recent jump in oil prices tied to Middle East tensions, and the labour market showing tentative signs of cooling, traders are unusually split on whether the next policy step is a hike or a hold. That uncertainty makes this week's data calendar, from today's ISM print through to Friday's non-farm payrolls, unusually important for setting the dollar's direction into the autumn, with knock-on effects for every other major currency covered here.
currencies.watchToday: The US ISM manufacturing PMI for July, due this afternoon, is today's key release, with markets looking for an improvement on June's 53.3 reading and watching the prices paid and new orders components closely for inflation and demand signals. It sets the tone for a data-heavy week that builds toward Wednesday's ADP employment report, Wednesday's ISM services PMI, and Friday's non-farm payrolls, the single biggest release of the week for the dollar.

currencies.headline: Yen extends a sharp rally after a hawkish BoJ hold and reports of coordinated intervention with Washington.
currencies.commentary:
The Japanese yen has continued to strengthen this morning, adding to a rapid multi-session advance that began after Friday's Bank of Japan decision. The Bank held its policy rate at 1.00% by an 8-1 vote, but board member Hajime Takata dissented in favour of an immediate move to 1.25%, and the Bank raised its fiscal 2026 growth forecast while flagging that underlying inflation is likely to move clearly above target later in the year. Adding to the move, Japan's Finance Ministry confirmed it carried out coordinated yen-buying operations with the US Treasury last week, a rare joint intervention that has amplified the currency's gains.

This matters because it marks a genuine shift in tone from Tokyo: verbal warnings about excessive weakness had done little to slow the yen's earlier slide, but an actual coordinated intervention alongside a hawkish dissent inside the Bank signals real discomfort with how far the currency had fallen. With the Bank of Japan and Federal Reserve now moving in less divergent directions than earlier this year, the yen looks better supported than it has in months, though the durability of the move will depend on whether the Bank follows through with an actual hike at a coming meeting.
currencies.watchToday: No major Japanese data is due today. Attention stays on any follow-through from Friday's Bank of Japan decision and the reported intervention, with Wednesday's release of the Bank's June meeting minutes offering a further look at how close the Board came to hiking before this month's hawkish dissent.

currencies.headline: Franc holds its safe-haven bid as Middle East tensions keep demand for havens elevated.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss franc has traded firmly overnight and into this morning, benefiting from its traditional role as a haven at a time when the latest flare-up in Middle East hostilities has kept broader risk sentiment cautious. The Swiss National Bank has held its policy rate at zero since June and has repeatedly signalled a willingness to intervene in currency markets should franc strength become excessive, but with inflation running at just 0.5% year on year and forecast to peak below 1%, there is little domestic pressure on the Bank to act. Today's July CPI print, due this morning, is one of the few scheduled pieces of Swiss data before the SNB's next quarterly decision in September.

The broader context matters here: Switzerland's comparatively stable economic and political backdrop, combined with elevated global debt levels and recurring geopolitical shocks, continues to funnel safe-haven flows into the franc, even though the SNB has downgraded its 2026 growth forecast to just under 1% on the back of higher US tariffs. That combination of low inflation, a patient central bank, and persistent haven demand leaves the franc structurally well supported, even if a cyclical recovery in Europe could take some of the edge off its strength later in the year.
currencies.watchToday: Swiss CPI for July, released this morning, is the main scheduled event and will feed directly into the SNB's assessment ahead of its September meeting. Beyond today, the calendar is thin for the franc this week, so haven flows tied to the Middle East situation are likely to remain the dominant driver.

currencies.headline: Loonie firmer as the latest jump in oil prices offsets a cautious growth backdrop.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has firmed modestly this morning, supported by the recent surge in crude prices after Iran and Israel traded strikes over the weekend, which has added a fresh risk premium to oil markets. That comes on the back of last week's surprisingly strong GDP data, with output rising 0.3% in May against an initial estimate of just 0.1%, and an advance estimate putting annualised second quarter growth at a robust 3.4%, a sharp rebound from the first quarter's mild contraction. The Bank of Canada has no meeting scheduled until early September, leaving the currency to trade mainly on oil and on the broader US dollar backdrop for now.

The connection between oil and the loonie is not always straightforward, but higher crude prices do tend to support Canada's terms of trade even as they add to domestic inflation through higher pump prices and refinery margins, a genuine two-sided effect the Bank of Canada has flagged explicitly in its recent policy communication. With growth data running hotter than expected and oil providing a tailwind, the currency looks reasonably well supported heading into a week where trade figures, rather than any central bank decision, will be the main domestic release.
currencies.watchToday: No major Canadian data is scheduled today. The week's key release is Tuesday's merchandise trade balance for June, watched as a barometer of cross-border demand and tariff related trade frictions, with the Bank of Canada not due to meet again until early September.

currencies.headline: Kiwi firm on hawkish RBNZ signals as traders await a critical labour market test.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has held a firm tone into this morning's session, extending gains built up over the past few weeks after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand delivered its first rate hike in three years at its July meeting. That move followed a hotter than expected inflation print, with annual CPI accelerating to 4.1% in the second quarter, above both the 4.0% consensus and the Bank's own 3.9% forecast, and markets now widely expect a further hike at the September meeting. There is no major New Zealand data due today, so the currency continues to trade largely on that hawkish RBNZ narrative alongside the broader risk backdrop shaped by Middle East developments and the US dollar.

The stakes are rising heading into tomorrow: strategists have pointed to above-target inflation and an improving domestic growth outlook as the key supports for further RBNZ tightening, but that view rests heavily on the labour market holding up. A weak reading tomorrow would raise real questions about how much further the Bank can realistically tighten without denting employment, making it arguably the single most important release for the currency this week.
currencies.watchToday: No major New Zealand data is due today. The week's pivotal release is tomorrow's second quarter employment and unemployment report, which lands just weeks after the RBNZ's hawkish pivot and will be watched closely for signs of whether the labour market can withstand further tightening.

currencies.headline: Aussie caught between a supportive RBA stance and an uneven Chinese recovery.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has traded steadily this morning, caught between two competing forces that have defined its recent path. On one hand, the Reserve Bank of Australia has held its cash rate in a wait-and-see stance, with markets pricing only around a one in four chance of a hike at its next meeting but better than even odds of one by year end, a supportive backdrop for the currency. On the other, China's official manufacturing PMI slipped back into contraction at 49.2 in July, well below the 50.0 consensus, and broader Chinese activity data showed retail sales growth slowing to just 1.0% year on year and fixed asset investment falling 5.7% in the first half, a genuine headwind for a currency so tied to commodity demand.

The mechanism linking the two matters directly for the Aussie: China remains Australia's largest trading partner and the main buyer of its iron ore and other commodity exports, so a cooling Chinese economy weighs on Australia's terms of trade even as domestic interest rate settings stay relatively supportive. That tug of war between a patient RBA and an uneven Chinese recovery is likely to keep the currency choppy and headline-driven, with Chinese data proving just as important to the Aussie's path as anything released domestically.
currencies.watchToday: No major Australian data is due today, though this morning's China Caixin manufacturing PMI, a private-sector gauge watched closely for its trade linkages to Australia, is relevant background after the weaker official Chinese PMI on Friday. The week's key domestic release is Thursday's trade balance, watched closely given China's outsized role as a buyer of Australian exports.

currencies.headline: Yuan steady as Beijing pushes ahead with reforms even as factory activity data sends mixed signals.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has traded in a tight, well contained range this morning, consistent with its recent pattern of stability even as the currency has been one of the better performers among major currencies so far in 2026. That stability comes despite a mixed picture on the factory floor: the official NBS manufacturing PMI slipped back into contraction at 49.2 in July, below the 50.0 consensus, while this morning's private sector Caixin manufacturing PMI, which tends to skew toward smaller export and tech oriented firms, offers a cross-check on whether that weakness is broad based. The People's Bank of China has continued to strike a supportive but cautious tone, with Governor Pan Gongsheng highlighting broadening international demand for the yuan without signalling any imminent shift in rates.

The bigger story is structural rather than cyclical: Beijing has been rolling out measures to cement Hong Kong's role as the main offshore hub for the yuan, including higher caps on cross-border trading and bond connect schemes, a long-term push toward internationalising the currency that sits somewhat apart from the near-term factory data. For now, that structural support and the PBoC's steady hand are keeping the yuan anchored within a well defined band, even as the divergence between the official and private manufacturing surveys leaves some uncertainty about the true state of Chinese industrial demand, a point with knock-on relevance for commodity currencies like the Australian and New Zealand dollars.
currencies.watchToday: This morning's Caixin manufacturing PMI for July is the main release, watched as a cross-check on Friday's weaker official NBS PMI reading, with the Caixin services PMI following on Wednesday. Beyond the data, the PBoC's ongoing structural reforms around Hong Kong's offshore yuan market remain the bigger medium-term theme for the currency.

currencies.headline: Rand steady as the SARB's surprise hold and rising inflation set a cautious tone.
currencies.commentary:
The South African rand has traded with a steady tone this morning, digesting last week's surprise decision by the South African Reserve Bank to leave its policy rate unchanged in a split 4-2 vote, a move markets had not fully priced in. That hold came even as annual inflation accelerated to 5.0% in June, the highest reading in two years and above the 4.7% consensus, driven mainly by transport and housing costs, leaving the Bank in a genuinely delicate position between supporting growth and containing price pressures. This morning's Absa/BER manufacturing PMI for July is the first data point of the new week and will give an early read on the health of the sector.

Governor Lesetja Kganyago used last Friday's Reserve Bank annual meeting to reaffirm the Bank's commitment to its new 3% inflation target while also warning that renewed conflict in the Middle East could add further inflation risk through higher oil and fertiliser prices, a reminder that global shocks are feeding directly into South Africa's domestic price outlook. With the SARB's next policy meeting not due until September, the rand is likely to keep trading on that inflation and global risk narrative, alongside broader dollar sentiment, rather than on any fresh domestic catalyst this week.
currencies.watchToday: The Absa/BER manufacturing PMI for July, due this morning, is today's only scheduled release and will offer an early signal on the sector's health. With the SARB not meeting again until September, the rand is likely to keep trading on last week's inflation surprise and on broader global risk sentiment, including any further escalation in the Middle East, for the rest of the week.

currencies.headline: Sterling shrugs off a much weaker UK factory PMI as broad dollar softness lends support.
currencies.commentary:
This morning's final UK manufacturing PMI landed well below expectations, revised down to a four month low as new order growth and hiring both cooled, a notably weaker outcome than the earlier flash estimate had suggested. On its own that would typically weigh on sterling, but the currency has instead traded with a firmer tone through the European afternoon, helped by the broader retreat in the dollar that followed confirmation of the joint US Japan intervention to support the yen. Cable has pushed toward its best level in a couple of weeks even as the domestic data disappointed, a reminder that external forces are currently doing more to move the pound than anything happening at home.

That divergence between soft UK data and a firmer pound says as much about the dollar's troubles as it does about British fundamentals. With the Bank of England on hold and no meeting scheduled this week, sterling is effectively trading as a proxy for dollar sentiment, and today's weak PMI print raises a small question mark over the strength of the recovery in UK manufacturing heading into Wednesday's services reading, which will offer a fuller picture of the domestic economy.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled for sterling specifically for the rest of today; the next data point lands just after midnight with the BRC shop price and retail sales monitors for July. The bigger test comes Wednesday with the UK's final services PMI, while this afternoon's US ISM manufacturing print is likely to matter more for cable in the short term than anything on the domestic calendar.

currencies.headline: Euro extends its advance as a firm PMI confirmation meets a broadly weaker dollar.
currencies.commentary:
This morning's final eurozone manufacturing PMI was confirmed a touch below the earlier flash estimate but still at its strongest reading since April, with German factory output reported at a four year high. That modestly encouraging confirmation has been overshadowed by the bigger story of the session, the broad dollar retreat that followed confirmation of coordinated US Japan intervention to support the yen, which has pushed the euro to its firmest level against the dollar in about six weeks. The single currency has held those gains through the European afternoon with little sign of profit taking so far.

The combination of resilient eurozone factory data and a softer dollar reinforces the case markets built last week for a European Central Bank that stays on hold for longer, after core inflation surprised to the upside. With the ECB's next meeting still some weeks away, the euro's near term path looks more tied to how the dollar story evolves than to fresh eurozone news, at least until Wednesday's services PMI and producer price figures provide the next real test.
currencies.watchToday: No further eurozone data is due for the rest of today. Wednesday brings the final services and composite PMIs alongside producer price figures, with Thursday's retail sales rounding out the week's releases, all of which will help confirm whether last week's hawkish inflation surprise has further to run.

currencies.headline: Dollar slips back as confirmation of the weekend's yen intervention overshadows this morning's steadier tone.
currencies.commentary:
The dollar has given back this morning's modest steadiness through the European afternoon, turning softer again as Japan's Finance Ministry and the US Treasury formally confirmed last week's coordinated intervention to support the yen, the first joint action of its kind since 2011. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reinforced the move by warning that Washington would not hesitate to join further coordinated action if needed, comments that have kept the dollar under broad pressure rather than just against the yen, with the euro and sterling both firmer as a result and Asian currencies mixed as markets digest the shift.

The bigger question for the dollar this afternoon is whether it can find its footing once the ISM manufacturing survey lands later today, the first major US data point of a week that builds toward Friday's payrolls report. A stronger than expected reading could help the currency stabilise after a rough stretch, while a miss would likely compound today's intervention driven weakness. Markets are also weighing what the renewed willingness to intervene signals about the administration's tolerance for further dollar declines.
currencies.watchToday: The US ISM manufacturing PMI for July, due this afternoon, is the key remaining release, with markets looking for an improvement on June's reading and watching the prices paid and new orders components closely. It kicks off a data heavy week that builds toward Wednesday's ISM services PMI and Fed minutes, and Friday's non farm payrolls.

currencies.headline: Yen holds the bulk of its intervention driven surge as Tokyo signals readiness to act again.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has held onto most of its recent sharp advance through the European afternoon, having jumped to its strongest level in around three months after Japan's Finance Ministry and the US Treasury confirmed last week's coordinated intervention to support the currency. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told reporters today that the authorities would not hesitate to act again, while Treasury Secretary Bessent backed the operation as a response to disorderly moves, comments that have helped the currency defend its gains through the session rather than drift back toward the multi decade lows hit before the intervention.

This marks the first coordinated US Japan intervention since 2011 and reflects growing discomfort in Washington as well as Tokyo with how far the yen had fallen, given the currency's slide to levels not seen since the 1980s and the knock on effect on the US trade deficit. With both sides now on record as willing to intervene again, the bar for a fresh bout of sharp yen weakness looks meaningfully higher than it did a week ago, even if the underlying interest rate gap that drove the decline remains largely intact.
currencies.watchToday: No Japanese data is due for the rest of today. Wednesday's release of the Bank of Japan's June meeting minutes is the next scheduled catalyst, offering a further look at how close the board came to raising rates before this month's hawkish dissent, though fresh intervention headlines remain the more immediate risk in either direction.

currencies.headline: Franc holds firm as a softer inflation print and a cautious risk mood reinforce its haven bid.
currencies.commentary:
Swiss inflation data released this morning came in softer than expected, with the annual rate easing from June's reading as fuel prices and airfares fell, while core inflation held steady. That undershoot has done nothing to dent the franc, which has instead traded firmly through the European afternoon alongside the yen as investors lean into haven currencies amid a genuinely unsettled session, with Asian equities mixed to sharply lower after the dollar's intervention driven wobble and South Korea's benchmark index posting a particularly steep decline overnight.

The soft inflation print further reduces any near term pressure on the Swiss National Bank to act, whether through rate changes or currency intervention, since price growth remains comfortably contained well below the levels troubling other major economies. With the SNB's next policy decision not due until September, the franc's path from here looks tied more to how broader risk sentiment and the dollar story evolve than to anything happening domestically.
currencies.watchToday: No further Swiss data is scheduled for the rest of today, and the calendar stays quiet for the franc through the rest of the week. Haven demand tied to the broader market mood, along with any follow through from today's yen intervention headlines, remains the more likely driver into tomorrow.

currencies.headline: Loonie gives back its morning gains as oil reverses sharply on ceasefire relief.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has turned softer through the European afternoon, unwinding the gains it made earlier in the session when crude prices spiked on reports of Iran and Israel trading strikes over the weekend. That early oil driven strength has reversed hard as signs the ceasefire is holding and Iranian barrels returning to the market have pulled crude sharply lower, with West Texas Intermediate giving back a large chunk of its recent advance. Since Canada remains one of the world's most oil sensitive currencies, the loonie has moved almost in lockstep with the swing in crude.

The round trip in oil prices, up sharply overnight then down just as sharply this afternoon, highlights how exposed the currency remains to swings in Middle East headlines even as the domestic backdrop stays relatively settled. Last week's stronger than expected GDP data and the Bank of Canada's more neutral tone have taken a back seat for now, with the currency likely to keep trading as a function of the oil market and geopolitical headlines rather than anything on the local calendar until tomorrow.
currencies.watchToday: No Canadian data is due for the rest of today. Tomorrow's merchandise trade balance for June is the next scheduled release and will be watched as a barometer of cross border demand, though oil prices and the durability of the Middle East ceasefire remain the dominant near term drivers.

currencies.headline: Kiwi holds its recent gains as broad dollar weakness adds to an already hawkish RBNZ backdrop.
currencies.commentary:
The New Zealand dollar has had a quiet but firm afternoon, with little fresh domestic news landing since this morning, extending the steady tone it has held since last month's stronger than expected inflation print and the Reserve Bank's first rate hike in three years. The broader retreat in the dollar following the confirmed US Japan yen intervention has added a modest extra tailwind, lifting most major currencies against the greenback simultaneously rather than reflecting anything specific to New Zealand.

With no domestic data due until tomorrow, the kiwi's next real test comes from the labour market rather than from today's session. Markets are already positioning for the possibility of another quarter point hike in September, and tomorrow's employment report will be the clearest signal yet of whether the jobs market can withstand further tightening without cracking, making it a considerably bigger event for the currency than anything left on today's calendar.
currencies.watchToday: New Zealand's second quarter employment and unemployment report, due late tomorrow evening UK time, is a high importance release and the clearest test yet of how the labour market is holding up under RBNZ tightening. Beyond that, broader risk sentiment and any further fallout from today's dollar weakness remain the other swing factors into tomorrow.

currencies.headline: Aussie stays capped by a soft Chinese PMI and a shaky regional equity mood despite the weaker dollar.
currencies.commentary:
The Australian dollar has struggled to fully capitalise on the broader dollar weakness this afternoon, held back by a private sector Chinese manufacturing survey published this morning that missed expectations and eased to its softest reading in several months, adding to Friday's disappointing official Chinese PMI. Asian equity markets were mixed to sharply lower overnight as the region digested the confirmed US Japan intervention, with South Korea's index tumbling more than five percent, and that cautious regional mood has left the Aussie trading in a narrow range rather than joining sterling and the euro in pushing meaningfully higher against the dollar.

The combination underlines how much the Australian dollar behaves as a proxy for Chinese growth sentiment, with two soft factory readings in the space of a few trading days reinforcing concerns about the health of its largest trading partner even as the Reserve Bank of Australia maintains a cautiously supportive stance. That tension between a resilient domestic policy backdrop and a wobblier China story looks set to keep the currency rangebound until fresh catalysts emerge.
currencies.watchToday: No Australian data is due for the rest of today. Thursday's trade balance is the next domestic release, though China's trade figures on Friday are likely to carry more weight for the Aussie given the size of the trading relationship.

currencies.headline: Yuan steady as a soft private sector PMI adds to Friday's weak official reading.
currencies.commentary:
A private sector gauge of Chinese manufacturing activity published this morning missed expectations and eased to its softest level in several months, though it stayed just above the growth threshold, adding to Friday's weaker official reading and reinforcing a picture of cooling momentum in China's factory sector. The offshore yuan has nonetheless remained well contained through the afternoon, with the People's Bank of China again setting its daily reference rate on the weaker side of where the market had expected, consistent with its recent pattern of leaning against further currency appreciation even as the dollar broadly retreats elsewhere.

The back to back soft PMI prints, official and private sector alike, sit somewhat awkwardly against the yuan's status as one of the better performing major currencies so far this year, and will likely feed into questions about whether Beijing needs to lean harder on stimulus to support growth. For now the central bank's tight grip on the daily fixing continues to keep the currency's day to day moves unusually contained regardless of what the underlying data shows.
currencies.watchToday: Nothing further is scheduled for the yuan for the rest of today. Wednesday's private sector services PMI is the next release, followed by Friday's trade balance figures, which will offer a fuller read on how external demand is holding up.

currencies.headline: Rand fails to fully ride the dollar's slide as risk-off cross-currents and seasonal caution weigh.
currencies.commentary:
This morning's Absa manufacturing PMI for July pointed to continued softness in South Africa's factory sector, extending a run of weak readings and offering little in the way of positive surprise. The rand has struggled to draw much lasting support from the broader dollar weakness that has lifted most other majors this afternoon following the confirmed US Japan intervention, with the currency's gains proving more muted than sterling's or the euro's as the cautious mood in Asian equity markets bleeds into risk appetite for emerging market currencies more broadly.

That relative underperformance fits a broader pattern for the rand, which enters August, historically its weakest month, still digesting last month's surprise decision by the Reserve Bank to leave rates unchanged despite inflation running at a two year high, and recent reports of foreign investors turning net sellers of local bonds. With domestic policy on hold until September, the currency looks more exposed than most to any wobble in broader risk appetite over the coming weeks.
currencies.watchToday: No further South African data is scheduled for the rest of today, and the calendar stays quiet for the rand through the rest of the week. Broader dollar sentiment and global risk appetite, rather than anything domestic, are likely to remain the main drivers into tomorrow.

currencies.headline: Sterling stays on the back foot as fiscal jitters overshadow yesterday's steady Bank of England hold.
currencies.commentary:
The pound has drifted lower overnight and into this morning, extending a pullback that began earlier in the week as gilt yields sit near multi-month highs. Yesterday's Bank of England decision, a widely expected hold at 3.75% for a fifth straight meeting, did little to change the picture, with focus instead on the government's search for flexibility within its fiscal rules ahead of the autumn budget. That fiscal uncertainty, rather than anything from the Bank, has been the dominant driver of sterling sentiment this week.

The mechanism here matters: rising gilt yields reflect investors demanding a bigger premium to hold UK government debt amid spending uncertainty, and that risk premium has been weighing on the currency even though higher yields would normally support it. Until the government's fiscal plans are clarified, likely not before the October budget, relief rallies in both gilts and the pound are likely to stay capped, leaving sterling more exposed to fiscal headlines than to the usual interest rate story for now.
currencies.watchToday: No UK data is scheduled for today. The week ahead brings only lower-tier releases: manufacturing PMI on Monday, construction PMI on Tuesday and services PMI on Wednesday, so sterling is likely to keep trading on fiscal policy headlines and broader gilt market moves rather than fresh data.

currencies.headline: Euro treads carefully into today's flash inflation data after yesterday's upside growth surprise.
currencies.commentary:
The euro has been broadly steady this morning as traders position for two closely watched releases due later today: the Eurozone flash CPI print for July and the flash unemployment rate. That follows yesterday's Q2 GDP flash estimate, which came in well ahead of forecasts and eased fears the bloc might post a second weak quarter in a row, with Germany's own growth figure also beating expectations. The single currency firmed modestly on that data but has since settled into a narrower range ahead of today's inflation numbers.
